method: AI/ML successes and limitations along four complexity axes. DOIs verified against the Crossref API (title, first author, year) on 2026-10-30. Abstracts from OpenAlex abstract_inverted_index or nature.com landing pages; full text from arXiv preprints, Nature Communications HTML, and an institutional PDF (Selz & Craig, DLR eLib), converted with pdftotext. Every quote was string-matched against the saved text by build_ai.py; checked_in_text is true only where that match succeeded. Where the number was read in an arXiv preprint of a journal paper, notes say so. Rows ai-16 and ai-29 are not-found placeholders. On 2026-10-30 rows ai-21 and ai-22 were moved from axis tails to closures (see their notes). On 2026-10-30 row ai-21 (DeVries et al. 2018) was removed as a contested exemplar and rows ai-30 and ai-31 were added from abstracts read in the main session.

rows.task: earthquake detection (template matching, not deep learning)
rows.baseline: standard Southern California Seismic Network catalog
rows.metric: factor more earthquakes than the standard catalog
rows.item: Quake Template Matching (QTM) catalog, southern California 2008-2017
rows.quantity: size of enhanced catalog relative to the routine catalog
rows.value_text: a catalog with 1.81 million earthquakes, a 10-fold increase
rows.quote: This effort resulted in a catalog with 1.81 million earthquakes, a 10-fold increase
rows.notes: Template matching (waveform cross-correlation against known events), NOT machine learning. Included as the non-ML reference point for how much signal lies below routine detection. Full text not open; abstract via OpenAlex.

rows.task: earthquake detection and phase picking (EQTransformer)
rows.baseline: existing catalog for the 2000 Tottori aftershock period (Japan)
rows.metric: factor more earthquakes detected and located, using under 1/3 of stations
rows.item: EQTransformer applied to 5 weeks of continuous data, 2000 Tottori earthquake
rows.quantity: ratio of events detected and located to the reference catalog
rows.value_text: two times more earthquakes using only a portion (less than 1/3) of seismic stations
rows.quote: we were able to detect and locate two times more earthquakes using only a portion (less than 1/3) of seismic stations
rows.notes: Single aftershock sequence, 5 weeks. Baseline is the agency catalog (JMA), as described in the paper; the abstract does not name it.

rows.task: seismic P and S arrival picking (PhaseNet)
rows.metric: F1 score for P and S picks on held-out NCEDC test waveforms
rows.item: PhaseNet, Northern California Earthquake Data Center analyst picks
rows.value_text: F1 0.896 for P and 0.801 for S, vs AR picker 0.558 (P) and 0.165 (S)
rows.quote: PhaseNet achieves an F1 score of 0.896 for P arrivals and 0.801 for S arrivals, which is substantially better than the AR picker
rows.notes: Read from arXiv v1 preprint (1803.03211); confirm the table against the GJI version before quoting. Trained on >700,000 analyst-labelled waveforms (abstract). In-domain test: same network, same region.

rows.task: global medium-range weather forecasting (GraphCast)
rows.metric: percent of verification targets where ML beat baseline
rows.quantity: share of 1380 verification targets with significantly better skill
rows.value_text: outperforms the most accurate operational deterministic systems on 90% of 1380 verification targets
rows.quote: GraphCast significantly outperforms the most accurate operational deterministic systems on 90% of 1380 verification targets
rows.notes: Trained on ERA5 reanalysis; skill computed against ERA5/HRES analyses. Targets are variable x level x lead-time combinations. See ai-09 and ai-10 for what this aggregate score hides.

rows.task: global medium-range weather forecasting (Pangu-Weather)
rows.metric: 5-day Z500 RMSE, Pangu-Weather (IFS: 333.7)
rows.value_text: RMSE of 5-day Z500 forecast of 296.7 vs 333.7 (operational IFS) and 462.5 (FourCastNet)
rows.quote: Pangu-Weather reports an RMSE of 5-day Z500 forecast of 296.7, significantly better than the operational IFS
rows.notes: Number read from the arXiv technical report 2211.02556 (title differs from the Nature paper); the Nature abstract (read) says only 'stronger deterministic forecast results on reanalysis data in all tested variables'. Same report: inference 'more than 10000x faster than operational IFS'. Verify the number in the Nature version before quoting.

rows.task: global probabilistic weather forecasting (GenCast)
rows.metric: percent of verification targets where ML beat baseline
rows.quantity: share of 1,320 targets with greater skill
rows.value_text: greater skill than ENS on 97.2% of 1,320 targets
rows.quote: It has greater skill than ENS on 97.2% of 1,320 targets we evaluated
rows.notes: Abstract also claims better prediction of extreme weather and tropical cyclone tracks (no number in abstract).

rows.task: earthquake detection on distributed acoustic sensing (PhaseNet-DAS)
rows.metric: factor more events detected across four DAS cables
rows.item: PhaseNet-DAS v1, semi-supervised, four DAS cables (California)
rows.quantity: ratio of detected events to PhaseNet detections
rows.value_text: PhaseNet-DAS v1 detects 2-5 times more events than PhaseNet across four DAS cables
rows.quote: PhaseNet-DAS v1 detects 2-5 times more events than PhaseNet across four DAS cables
rows.notes: Labels are pseudo-labels from PhaseNet refined by GaMMA association; the paper states it has no manual labels as ground truth, so detections are checked against standard catalogs rather than scored with precision/recall. Same text: v2 adds 25-50% sensitivity over v1; associated-pick rate 59-69% (PhaseNet) vs 89-92% (PhaseNet-DAS).

rows.task: InSAR time-series deformation detection (deep autoencoder)
rows.baseline: conventional InSAR analysis with expert interpretation and prior fault knowledge
rows.metric: detection threshold for ground deformation
rows.item: North Anatolian Fault InSAR time series
rows.value_text: reaches 2 mm detection, revealing a slow earthquake twice as extensive as previously recognized
rows.quote: our method reaches 2 mm detection, revealing a slow earthquake twice as extensive as previously recognized
rows.notes: Trained on synthetic deformation plus realistic atmospheric noise; one fault segment plus Coso geothermal test. 'Twice as extensive' is spatial extent vs earlier InSAR/creepmeter studies. Could also sit under 'unobserved' (no prior fault location needed).

rows.task: global medium-range weather forecasting (Pangu-Weather spectra)
rows.baseline: ERA5 analysis spectra; ECMWF IFS forecasts
rows.metric: effective resolution (wavelength where kinetic energy spectrum departs from ERA5)
rows.quantity: effective horizontal resolution vs nominal 0.25 deg (~28 km)
rows.value_text: effective resolution of Pangu-Weather forecasts is closer to 500-700 km than to the nominal 0.25 deg
rows.quote: the effective resolution of PanguWeather forecasts is closer to 500-700 km than to the nominal 0.25 deg
rows.notes: Read from arXiv 2309.08473 (title 'On some limitations of data-driven weather forecasting models'; GRL title differs). Same text: Pangu vertical velocities about 40% smaller than ERA5 hindcasts. Interpretation: the learned model occupies a much lower effective dimension than its output grid, i.e. it smooths mesoscale variance.

rows.task: error growth from small initial perturbations (Pangu-Weather)
rows.baseline: ICON physics-based model incl. convection-permitting run
rows.metric: underestimate of 72 h difference kinetic energy (DKE) growth for 0.1% amplitude perturbations
rows.item: Pangu-Weather, 300 hPa DKE, case of 26 June 2021
rows.quantity: orders of magnitude by which DKE growth is underestimated over 3 days
rows.value_text: underestimation of the DKE by five orders of magnitude compared to ICON
rows.quote: Over the three days, this leads to an underestimation of the DKE by five orders of magnitude compared to ICON.
rows.notes: Single case, one AI model. The AI model misses the butterfly effect (small-scale, fast error growth); for realistic-amplitude perturbations (100%) it 'basically agrees' with physics models (abstract). Shows the learned dynamics lack the small-scale degrees of freedom.

rows.task: neural-network subgrid convection and cloud parameterization (NNCAM)
rows.metric: speed-up of the physical parameterization
rows.quantity: factor by which NN parameterization is faster than SPCAM physics
rows.value_text: physical parameterization of NNCAM is 20 times faster than SPCAM and 8 times faster than CTRLCAM; total model speed-up factor 10
rows.quote: The physical parameterization of NNCAM is 20 times faster than SPCAM and 8 times faster than CTRLCAM.
rows.notes: arXiv 1806.04731 read. Abstract (read via OpenAlex): multiyear prognostic runs stable, reproduce mean climate, precipitation extremes and equatorial wave spectrum. Aquaplanet, fixed SST; later studies (not checked here) report online instability for other configurations.

rows.task: neural-network subgrid parameterization under warming (NNCAM)
rows.metric: SST warming at which the reference-trained network fails
rows.item: NNCAM trained on reference climate only
rows.value_text: NNCAM trained on reference climate only is unable to generalize to much warmer climates (+4K SST)
rows.quote: A look at the mean heating rates for the +4K SST simulation reveals that the ITCZ signal is washed out
rows.notes: Fixed by training on reference plus +4K data (NNCAM-ref+4K), i.e. by covering the target climate, not by extrapolation. Abstract: 'struggles to cope with temperatures far outside its training manifold'.

rows.task: hybrid differentiable dynamical core with learned physics (NeuralGCM) climate run
rows.metric: RMSE of global mean 850 hPa temperature in AMIP-style run (climatology: 0.45 K)
rows.value_text: ensemble mean temperature RMSE for NeuralGCM stands at 0.16K ... climatology's RMSE of 0.45K
rows.quote: The ensemble mean temperature RMSE for NeuralGCM stands at 0.16K when benchmarked against ERA5
rows.notes: Read from arXiv 2311.07222 (preprint); check Nature version. Same text: NeuralGCM-1.4 deg simulates 70,000 simulation days in 24 h on one TPU vs 19 simulated days on 13,824 CPU cores (X-SHiELD). Abstract: competitive with ECMWF ENS at 1-15 days.

rows.task: hybrid GCM (NeuralGCM) under imposed SST warming
rows.metric: SST increase at which NeuralGCM response diverges
rows.value_text: for more substantial SST increases (+4K), NeuralGCM's response diverges from expectations
rows.quote: for more substantial SST increases (+4K), NeuralGCM’s response diverges from expectations
rows.notes: Same preprint also notes climate drift with increased SST. Nature abstract (read): 'our model does not extrapolate to substantially different future climates'.

rows.task: laboratory earthquake time-to-failure from acoustic emission (random forest)
rows.baseline: naive model using only event periodicity
rows.metric: coefficient of determination R^2 of time-to-failure prediction (naive: 0.3)
rows.item: biaxial shear experiment, continuous acoustic emission
rows.value_text: R2 value of 0.89 (naive periodicity model: 0.3)
rows.source: Rouet-Leduc et al. (2017), Geophysical Research Letters
rows.quote: the time to failure predictions from the RF model are highly accurate, with an R2 value of 0.89
rows.notes: Read from arXiv 1702.05774. Periodic lab stick-slip, one apparatus. Learned statistical mapping, not a friction law. Transfer to Earth: Rouet-Leduc et al. (2019, Nat. Geosci., doi 10.1038/s41561-018-0274-6, abstract read) tracks Cascadia slow-slip displacement rate from tremor-like signal; abstract gives no number.

rows.task: learned friction or rheology closure with a stated skill number
rows.metric: not found
rows.item: learned rate-and-state friction law or rheology closure
rows.quantity: skill of a learned friction closure
rows.value_text: not found
rows.notes: One web search (2026-10-30) returned neural-network rate-and-state work (PINNs on stick-slip data, Scientific Reports 2024; RNN friction on synthetic data, arXiv 2402.14148; Caltech thesis 2025) but none read and no number checked. evidence_type set to success only because the field is required; treat as an open gap.

rows.task: forecasting record-breaking heat, cold and wind (deterministic AI models)
rows.metric: direction of RMSE difference on record-breaking events across lead times
rows.item: GraphCast, GraphCast operational, Pangu-Weather, Pangu-Weather operational, FuXi; test year 2020
rows.quantity: number of 2020 heat records evaluated (cold 32,991; wind 53,345)
rows.value_text: HRES still consistently outperforms state-of-the-art AI models ...; 162,751 heat, 32,991 cold, and 53,345 wind records
rows.quote: For the year 2020, this yields 162, 751 heat, 32, 991 cold, and 53, 345 wind records
rows.notes: Published title: 'Physics-based models outperform AI weather forecasts of record-breaking extremes' (Zhang, Fischer, Zscheischler, Engelke); arXiv 2508.15724 title begins 'Numerical models outperform'. The performance result is graphical; the text states no single RMSE gap. Text: AI errors 'grow almost linearly' with record exceedance, suggesting 'an implicit cap in AI forecasts around the most extreme training observation'. Quote has pdftotext spacing in thousands separators. Compare ai-18. Watson (2022, ERL, doi 10.1088/1748-9326/ac9d4e, abstract read) is the earlier review making the same point qualitatively, no number.

rows.task: probabilistic forecasting of record-breaking heat extremes (WeatherNext2, WeatherGen)
rows.baseline: ECMWF IFS ensemble (raw); EMOS post-processed IFS
rows.metric: Brier skill score over the IFS ensemble for record-breaking heat events at 72 h
rows.quantity: Brier skill score vs IFS ensemble
rows.value_text: WeatherNext2 achieves Brier skill scores over the IFS of 23% at the 90th percentile and 24% (23-26%) for record-breaking extreme events
rows.quote: WeatherNext2 achieves Brier skill scores over the IFS of 23% at the 90th percentile and 24% (23-26%) for record-breaking extreme events
rows.notes: Not peer reviewed (posted 2026-10-14); no Crossref DOI. Directly rebuts ai-17: argues deterministic-vs-deterministic verification of records is unsuitable. Same text: at 72 h CRPS improvement over IFS 25% (WeatherNext2), 17% (WeatherGen), 14% (EMOS). Heat only.

rows.task: forecasting out-of-distribution Category 5 tropical cyclones (FourCastNet)
rows.baseline: FourCastNet trained on full ERA5 1979-2015; ERA5 truth
rows.metric: minimum forecast central pressure reached by model trained without Category 3-5 storms
rows.quantity: forecast mslp floor (Cat 5 threshold in ERA5 <970 hPa)
rows.value_text: mslp barely reaches below 980 hPa
rows.quote: the intensification in FourCastNet-noTC’s forecasts slows dramatically and mslp barely reaches below 980 hPa
rows.notes: Read from arXiv 2410.14932. Training removed samples with tropical mslp below 988 hPa (25th percentile). Model forecasts a Category 3 instead of Category 5: a false negative with no signal of failure. Partial success: training without Cat 3-5 in one basin still gave some skill in that basin (generalization across basins).

rows.task: real-time earthquake magnitude estimation for early warning (TEAM-LM transformer)
rows.baseline: catalog magnitude (MA Chile, ML Italy, MJMA Japan)
rows.metric: magnitude above which estimates saturate (Italy 5.5, Chile 6.0, Japan none up to 7)
rows.value_text: saturation starts ... around 5.5 for Italy and 6.0 for Chile
rows.source: Munchmeyer et al. (2021), Geophysical Journal International
rows.quote: the saturation starts at different magnitudes, which are around 5.5 for Italy and 6.0 for Chile
rows.notes: Author name is Muenchmeyer (u-umlaut). Attributed to too few large training events; Japan (training set incl. 2011 Tohoku) shows no obvious bias up to M7. Same text: Mousavi & Beroza (2020, GRL, 10.1029/2019GL085976) single-station model saturated around M3 (secondhand, not read in that paper). Transfer learning from other regions mitigates.

rows.task: spatial aftershock forecasting (logistic regression vs deep learning)
rows.baseline: DeVries et al. (2018) deep neural network (AUC 0.85, 13,451 parameters)
rows.metric: AUC of a 2-parameter logistic regression on distance and mainshock slip
rows.value_text: AUC = 0.85 using 2 free parameters versus the 13,451 parameters ...; improved AUC = 0.86
rows.quote: measured distance and mainshock average slip can be used instead of stress, yielding an improved AUC = 0.86
rows.notes: Critiques DeVries et al. (2018, Nature, doi 10.1038/s41586-018-0438-y), which was removed from this table on 2026-10-30 as a contested exemplar. As of 2026-10-30 Nature and Crossref show a Matters Arising (this paper) and a Reply (Meade 2019), no retraction. Moved from tails to closures on 2026-10-30: the task learns where aftershocks occur from stress change, a learned closure, not event size. Brief Communication Arising. Abstract text read via OpenAlex. Shows matched skill with ~6,700x fewer parameters (2 vs 13,451); the DNN adds no predictive skill over simple stress or distance metrics.

rows.task: building footprint extraction from 50 cm satellite imagery (Open Buildings, Africa)
rows.metric: number of building footprints detected
rows.value_text: 516M Africa-wide detected footprints
rows.quote: was used to create the Open Buildings dataset of 516M Africa-wide detected footprints
rows.notes: No journal version or Crossref DOI found. Exposure data where cadastral data are missing. Test-set mAP@0.5IoU 0.657 overall, urban 0.613 (Fig. 9), so a large share of footprints are imperfect. Later releases extend coverage (not checked).

rows.task: building footprint extraction (Open Buildings, Africa) imagery coverage
rows.metric: share of African land surface with high-resolution imagery available for inference
rows.value_text: 19.4M km2, 64% of the land surface of the continent
rows.quote: available high-resolution satellite imagery in Africa (19.4M km2 , 64% of the land surface of the continent)
rows.notes: The other 36% has no inference at all. Recall not estimable from their extra evaluation set ('can be used for estimating precision, but not recall'). Quote spacing as in pdftotext.

rows.task: global building footprint extraction (Microsoft / Bing Maps)
rows.metric: number of building footprints detected worldwide
rows.value_text: We have detected 1.4B buildings from Bing Maps imagery between 2014 and 2024
rows.quote: We have detected **1.4B** buildings from Bing Maps imagery between 2014 and 2024
rows.notes: Not peer reviewed; a living dataset whose count changes. README also: false-positive rate ~1-2% per region (early 2022 samples).

rows.task: global building footprint extraction (Microsoft), regional recall
rows.metric: recall of building matches in Africa (Europe: 85.9%)
rows.value_text: Africa precision 94.4%, recall 70.9% (Europe 94.3% / 85.9%)
rows.notes: About 29% of labelled African buildings missed vs about 14% in Europe: exposure is least observed where it is least mapped. Evaluation set size and date not given in the README table. Quote is the table row.

rows.task: deep-learning-picked catalog revealing activated fault structures (central Italy 2016-2017)
rows.baseline: routine catalog of the local monitoring agency (INGV)
rows.metric: size of ML-based catalog (an order of magnitude more events than routine)
rows.value_text: catalog of ~900,000 earthquakes ... an order of magnitude more events than the catalog routinely produced
rows.source: Tan et al. (2021), The Seismic Record
rows.quote: build a high-precision catalog of ∼900,000 earthquakes spanning a 1 yr period, based on arrival times derived using a deep-neural-network-based picker
rows.notes: Abstract: reveals 'a large number of kilometer-long faults and diffuse seismicity' activated during the sequence, i.e. structures not in fault maps. Agency named as 'local earthquake monitoring agency' in abstract.

rows.task: cross-domain transfer of deep-learning seismic detectors (regional to teleseismic)
rows.baseline: in-domain performance of the same models (AUC 0.85-0.99)
rows.metric: maximum detection AUC on teleseismic GEOFON data for models trained on regional data
rows.item: six DL pickers, eight datasets (SeisBench benchmark)
rows.value_text: no model trained on a regional dataset reaches an AUC score above 0.75 for detection on GEOFON ... in-domain performance of 0.85 to 0.99
rows.source: Munchmeyer et al. (2022), JGR Solid Earth
rows.quote: no model trained on a regional dataset reaches an AUC score above 0.75 for detection on GEOFON
rows.notes: Value is an upper bound ('no model ... above 0.75'). Regional-to-regional transfer showed only mild degradation (abstract). Distribution shift here is source-receiver distance and frequency content.

rows.task: population or exposure mapping with ML and a stated accuracy
rows.metric: not found
rows.value_text: not found
rows.notes: Not searched in depth in this pass (time). Candidates: Meta High Resolution Settlement Layer (Tiecke et al. 2017, arXiv 1712.05839), WorldPop random-forest dasymetric maps. evidence_type field required; treat as an open gap.

rows.task: earthquake forecasting with a neural temporal point process (RECAST)
rows.metric: training-catalog size above which RECAST beats ETAS
rows.quantity: minimum training-set size for improved fit and forecast accuracy over ETAS
rows.value_text: improved fit and forecast accuracy compared to our benchmark when the training set is sufficiently long (>10^4 events)
rows.source: Dascher-Cousineau et al. (2023), Geophysical Research Letters
rows.quote: improved fit and forecast accuracy compared to our benchmark when the training set is sufficiently long (>10 4 events)
rows.notes: Abstract read via the OpenAlex API in the main session on 2026-10-30; the superscript renders as "10 4" in the extracted text. Also a data requirement: below about 10^4 events the advantage is not claimed.

rows.metric: lowest input magnitude at which the neural model kept skill while ETAS degraded
rows.value_text: both models perform similarly above M3; lowering the threshold to M1.2 reduces the performance of ETAS unlike the neural model
rows.quote: lowering the threshold to M1.2 reduces the performance of ETAS unlike the neural model
rows.notes: Abstract read via the OpenAlex API in the main session on 2026-10-30. Authors attribute part of the gain to handling incomplete data; target events M3+.
